E0952.summary: The voice of Deuteronomy, cited by Atwood to warn those favoured in the work against presumption and forgetting God in prosperity.
E0952.body: Atwood cites the Lawgiver (footnote: Deuteronomy 8:10) on the Israelites' suffering for rebellion and the warning against forgetting God in prosperity: “Beware that thou forget not the Lord thy God” [IV.3 ¶57; IV.3 n26]. She applies it by analogy to those favoured in the work, as a warning against presumption; she endorses it.

E0953.summary: The scientific laws of the Art, whose study together with the Hermetic records Atwood makes the needed foundation before any trial.
E0953.body: Atwood names the “study of the Hermetic records and scientific Laws of Art” [IV.3 ¶54] as the foundation required before anyone attempts a trial of the work.

E0954.summary: Rabbinical voices cited by Atwood, with endorsement as Hermetic, for creation from nothing understood as from the primitive non-Being, Wisdom.
E0954.body: Atwood cites the learned Rassbi (the Rabbi), Ben Jochai and his disciples in support of creation from nothing as from the primitive non-Being, which is Wisdom: “by non-Being they mean that which is neither conceivable as cause nor as essence, but yet is in fact the Cause of causes” [III.2 ¶31; III.2 ¶32]. She endorses the view as Hermetic. A footnote marker (29) at this point has no footnote in the chunk.

E0955.summary: The assimilating ferment by which bodies are transformed, spiritualized and preserved; Atwood also invokes purging out the old leaven.
E0955.body: Atwood treats leaven as the assimilating ferment by which bodies are transformed, spiritualized and preserved; bodies are “preserved by the assimilating must or leaven” [III.3 ¶23], which makes must another name for it. The old leaven is to be purged: “Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump” [III.3 ¶23].

E0956.summary: In Palingenius' Latin verse, the ethereal stone that the worthiest art fashions, forbidden to the profane and granted to few.
E0956.body: In Latin verse quoted from Palingenius, the Lepidem Aetherium is the object of the worthiest art, to be fashioned: “Fingendi Lepidem Aetherium, quem scire profanes Haud quaquam licet” [IV.3 ¶55]. It is forbidden to the profane, sought in vain by the wicked and granted to few. Translation (ours): “Ethereal Stone”; the book gives none.

E0957.summary: The first, popular grade of initiation, open to all, revealing only the internal life and ending with the soul on the borders of Tartarus.
E0957.body: For Atwood the Lesser Mysteries are the first grade of initiation. In them, it appears, the revelations of the natural spirit's first sphere were passed: “passing these, as it appears, in the Lesser Mysteries” [II.2 ¶8]. It was “the only popular initiation open to all” [II.3 ¶3], revealing only the internal life, a field of natural contemplation without rule. It ended with the soul on the borders of the Stygian lake in view of Tartarus: “And here the Lesser Mysteries ended” [II.3 ¶36].

E0958.summary: In the mysterious adeptest's words, the lesser world is the father of the Son, or what the Son is likened to; possibly linked with the microcosm.
E0958.body: The mysterious adeptest, quoted by Atwood, says the Son is “consubstantial nevertheless, and like his father the lesser world” [III.3 ¶50]. The phrase may name the lesser world as the Son's father or only liken the Son to it. The same passage calls the Stone “wonderfully salutary to the microcosm in universal triunity” [III.3 ¶50], but the text does not explicitly identify the microcosm with the lesser world. Not defined further.

E0959.summary: In Agrippa's words, the drink of forgetfulness that is to be cast out.
E0959.body: Agrippa, quoted by Atwood: “Cast out the drink of Lethe” [II.4 ¶19]. Lethe is the drink of forgetfulness.

E0960.summary: Atwood calls Life the nucleus of the whole Hermetic Mystery.
E0960.body: Atwood: “And Life is the nucleus of the whole Hermetic Mystery” [IV.4 ¶32].

E0961.summary: A secret binding of natures, paired with their magical dissolution, which Atwood says Bacon discovered; not explained.
E0961.body: Atwood credits Bacon with discovering “the secret ligature of natures, and their magical dissolution” [I.1 ¶38]. The text does not explain it further.

E0962.summary: The hidden, self-multiplying formal Light that perfects matter, is the Form of Gold and the Key of the Hermetic Mystery, and is to be freed.
E0962.body:
**Physical role.** An adept quoted by Atwood says “It is the Light only that can be truly multiplied, for this ascends and descends from the first fountain of multiplication and generation” [I.2 ¶8]; once perfected by art it exalts any body in its kind. Atwood makes it the forming, fermenting agent: “Light is the true fermental principle which perfects the Ether in its proper kind” [I.2 ¶44]; “This Form is Light, the source of central heat” [I.2 ¶45]; “the universal magnet of its own infinite self-multiplicative Light” [I.2 ¶48]. Albertus Magnus (via Becher) calls it “Light, which is the formal essence of all things, and most abundant in gold” [III.2 n38].

**Hidden and to be freed.** “To find this Light, and to free it from captivity” [III.1 ¶11] was the adepts' aim: “the Central Light and Wisdom was all their aim” [III.1 ¶13]. It is “not common Light, but that which in the first rotary wheel of life becomes efficient” [IV.3 ¶30], latent in every kingdom of nature; Atwood asks, “is not Light the true Aurific Seed” [IV.3 ¶30], and calls it the Stone's own metal, its ferment. “that ray of motive Light, pure, vital, and efficient, we have shown to be the true Form of Gold” [IV.4 ¶9]; Nature is to “establish a stable monarchy upon her redeemed Light” [IV.4 ¶6].

**Inner and divine.** All Nature is its Efflux [III.3 ¶78]; Thought emanates it [III.3 ¶79]; recreation is “a stupendous metaphysical birth out of the Infinite into Light” [III.3 ¶79], with “reason BECOMING A BRIGHT Light” [III.3 ¶80]. The practice develops “by rational inquisition of the Light within” [IV.1 ¶18]; “Some have met the Light sooner, some later” [IV.1 ¶17]; one passes “by a living experience into the Light” [III.4 ¶15]. Quoting Plotinus, the soul receives a sudden Light: “For the Light is with Power, and is God.” [IV.2 ¶41]; Atwood also calls the magistery “a fiery form of Light inspisate” [IV.2 ¶37].

**Key.** “the Key thereof is Light” [IV.4 ¶32]; Atwood says “we pretend only to have signalized the Light” [IV.4 ¶2], and that she has shown “the golden ore” of it [IV.4 ¶32]; “for those to whom it is addressed the Light will attract” [IV.4 ¶31]. The selfish “have willfully denied the Light its true fulfillment” [III.4 ¶6]; in its vision the philosophers despised gold and silver [IV.3 ¶26]. In the later Appendix (Table Talk), “It requires Light to throw Light upon Light” [APP ¶118]; it is “the light which comes into every soul born into the world” [APP ¶126].

E0963.summary: In the theosophist's words, the other principle in everything, the woman's seed, to be raised up to shine through and subdue the wrath.
E0963.body: The theosophist, quoted by Atwood, names “the woman’s seed the light and love fire” [IV.3 ¶38]: the other principle in every thing, which must be raised up to shine through and subdue the wrath.

E0964.summary: What the quintessences lack, so that they resolve and die (Appendix).
E0964.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says quintessences “uninformed with the Light Essential, resolve and die” [APP ¶23]. Not further defined.

E0965.summary: What Atwood says is discovered by inquiring into the substance and practical evolution of the psychical experience.
E0965.body: Atwood: “It is into the substantiality of this and for its practical evolution that we must inquire, if we would discover the true Light of Alchemy” [II.1 ¶47]; the “this” is the psychical experience.

E0966.summary: In Boehme's words, the Light needed to understand the Tincture, which nature cannot grasp by its own ability.
E0966.body: Boehme, quoted by Atwood: “the understanding and capacity is not in nature’s own ability without the Light of God” [III.2 ¶16]. To those in it the matter is plain: “it is very easy to be understood by those who are in the Light” [III.2 ¶16].

E0967.summary: The light exhibited in the true Eleusinian initiations, which they could kindle and fortify.
E0967.body: Atwood: “The light exhibited in the Eleusinian msteries, i.e., in the true initiations as is plainly to be gathered from the sense of the ancients, was the Light of Life” [II.4 ¶56], the light “which these could kindle and fortify” [II.4 ¶56].

E0968.summary: In Sendivogius' words, nature's own light, hidden by the body of sense, which when it enlightens someone clears the cloud and penetrates inward things.
E0968.body: Sendivogius, quoted by Atwood: “nature, having her proper light, is by the shadowy body of sense, hidden from our eyes” [II.1 ¶10]. When “the light of nature doth enlighten any one, presently the cloud is taken away from before his eyes” [II.1 ¶10]; “so far doth the light of nature penetrate and discover inward things” [II.1 ¶10]. The philosophers see all things in it as in a mirror.

E0969.summary: The light that flows into and purifies the aerial moisture and re-enters in the Mysteries; Atwood identifies it with the Sulfur of adepts.
E0969.body: Atwood speaks of the aerial moisture “before it is purified by the inflowing light of reason” [II.3 ¶29], and of “the re-entering Light of Reason in the Mysteries, which is that Sulfur of adepts” [II.3 ¶30]. The ignorant scoffer lacks it, and so “without the Light of Reason, would be least of all able to precipitate its downfall” [IV.3 ¶56].

E0970.summary: The light kindled by the catholic torch; not further defined.
E0970.body: Atwood says the catholic torch “kindles the Light of Universal Nature” [IV.4 ¶32]. Not further defined.

E0971.summary: Our present life going forth in a line, which must be taken up into a circle back to its first source (Appendix).
E0971.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “Our life goes forth into a line at present, it has to be taken up into a circle” [APP ¶48], that is, back into its first source.

E0972.summary: The single uniform course of dissolution throughout the work, in one matter and one vessel, which the Adepts also call Manual.
E0972.body: Atwood describes “one linear decoction throughout and dissolution by line” [IV.1 ¶3] and “one linear way throughout” [IV.1 ¶9], in one matter and one vessel. It is “called by the Adepts Manual, and their Linear way” [IV.1 ¶5]. Not further explained.

E0973.summary: In the words of the fraternity of the Rosy Cross, the creature whose blood, joined with the Eagle's tears, is the treasure of the whole earth.
E0973.body: In the fraternity of the Rosy Cross, quoted by Atwood, the Lion is the other creature; weakened, it bleeds: “The blood of this Lion incorporated with the tears of the Eagle is the treasure of the whole earth.” [III.3 ¶63]. A green and red lion is drawn from the Dragon's body. Not further explained.

E0974.summary: In The Hunting of the Greene Lyon, the liquid given to the pure matter at each imbibition.
E0974.body: The verse *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon*, quoted by Atwood: “A portion of your Lyons sweate Must be given it for to eate:” [III.1 ¶65], i.e. at each imbibition of the pure matter. Not further defined; how it relates to the Lion's Blood is unclear.

E0975.summary: In Eudoxus' words, the liquor hidden under the Stone that contains all the work needs, which has over a thousand names and is the great Alcahest.
E0975.body: Eudoxus, quoted by Atwood: “search the source of the Liquor of the Sages, which contains all that is necessary for the work; it is hidden under the Stone” [IV.3 ¶10]. He calls it “this precious liquor, to which the philosophers have given more than a thousand different names, which is in sum the great Alcahest” [IV.3 ¶10]. Whether it is the liquor from which the two Mercuries are made is not stated.

E0977.summary: What the Quintessence becomes with the Divine light's virtue: transmuting, multiplicative gold, the concrete form of what is valued in dead metal.
E0977.body: Atwood: with the virtue of the Divine light the Quintessence becomes “the living gold of the philosophers, transmuting and multiplicative --- the concrete form of that which in the dead metal we esteem” [III.1 ¶49].

E0978.summary: The Light which, Atwood says, became known to Solomon together with the mysteries of universal creation.
E0978.body: Atwood says Solomon “celebrates the revelation of that Living Light which became known to him” [III.3 ¶49], together with the mysteries of universal creation.

E0979.summary: The inner place, guarded by the adepts' equivocations, where the wise raise the Corner Stone and where desire is addressed from the Divine Light within.
E0979.body: Atwood: the adepts' equivocations protect “that living temple wherein alone the wise of all ages have been securely able to raise their rejected Corner Stone” [II.1 ¶8]. Effectual desire is “addressed within the Living Temple from the Divine Light within” [III.4 ¶27]. The context suggests an inner place; it is not further defined.

E0980.summary: Author of the Essay, cited by Atwood in support of intuition as the highest certainty, though she criticizes his 'sensual system'.
E0980.body: Atwood cites Locke's *Essay* in support of intuition as the highest certainty: “Intuitive faith is certain beyond all doubt, and needs no proof beyond itself” [II.1 ¶34]. She also criticizes Locke's 'sensual system', so her endorsement is partial.

E0981.summary: An image of attraction and a cover-name: the enlightened see the point of the philosophers' lodestone; Cosmopolite gives the name to the Mercury.
E0981.body: Agrippa and Sendivogius, quoted by Atwood, use it as an image of attraction. Man is to “draw and bring them to himself as a loadstone, iron” [II.1 ¶9]. The enlightened man “can behold the point of our lodestone, answering to each center of the beams” [II.1 ¶10] of the philosophical sun and moon. Eirenaeus (“the same author”) prescribes “conjoin to nine parts of our Lodestone” [IV.1 ¶43] with the Fiery Dragon; not explained. Eudoxus reports that Cosmopolite gives the Mercury (Our Old Man) “also the name of steel and of the lodestone” [IV.3 ¶10]. In a passage of unclear voice, “as steel draws the loadstone and the loadstone in like manner turns toward steel” [IV.2 ¶30] is compared to freed Will and Understanding; our loadstone has Salt at its center, turning to the Pole, and our Magnet shows “that Polar Star which our Magnet exhibits” [IV.2 ¶30].

E0982.summary: Used by Atwood of those whom Ripley's Twelve Gates edified; apparently an inner circle of the initiated.
E0982.body: Atwood says Ripley's Twelve Gates “little edified any without the Lodge” [I.1 ¶64]. The context suggests the Lodge is an inner circle of the initiated, but the text does not say so; other readings are possible.
